Chapter 6: Prevention—Strategies for Avoiding the Sidepiece Trap
Now that we’ve talked about self-awareness and building a good support system, let’s take a look at how you can actually avoid falling into the sidepiece trap from the very start.
Prevention isn’t about blaming yourself or anyone else. It's really about giving yourself the tools you need to spot red flags early, and to make choices that fit your values—and your long-term happiness.
The first big idea here is all about discernment, especially when you’re just starting to get to know someone. Think of it as tuning into the subtle signals—like when someone gives you vague answers, dodges questions about their life, or seems hesitant to let you meet their friends or family.
And if their schedule always seems... off? Like they’re only free at odd hours, or can never commit to plans in advance? That could be a sign there’s something they’re not telling you.
So, how do you stay out of the sidepiece zone? Here are a few real-world strategies:
First, ask direct questions. Don’t be afraid to have honest conversations early on—about relationship status, past commitments, and what you both really want. It might feel a little uncomfortable at first, but these talks can reveal a lot, fast.
Second, watch what they do—not just what they say. Words are easy, but actions? That’s where the truth shows up. If someone’s promises and actual behavior don’t line up, that’s your cue to slow down and pay attention.
Third, set your own non-negotiable boundaries. Decide ahead of time what you’re okay with—and what you’re not. Maybe you won’t accept secrecy, last-minute plans, or someone being evasive about their life. Sticking to these boundaries can really help protect you from sliding into a role you never wanted.
And finally, trust your gut. If something feels off, it probably is. Intuition is a powerful tool—especially when you combine it with what you’re seeing and hearing.
Let’s put this into perspective. Imagine you notice a new partner never picks up the phone in the evening. Or maybe they dodge sharing their social media, or just never invite you to meet their friends. In these moments, stepping back and asking for clarity isn’t just smart—it’s self-care.
Or say you’re the one who insists on meeting friends or being included in public plans. By doing that, you quickly learn if the relationship is genuinely open—or if there’s something being hidden.
Here’s something to remember: prevention isn’t about being paranoid. It’s really about respecting yourself enough to stay clear and honest about what you want. If you approach new relationships with openness and discernment, you’ll be in a much better place to avoid the pain and confusion of being someone’s secret—or second choice.
